Ward (github.com/MuhammadMurtuzaHussain/ward, public MIT, local checkout at `/Users/haider/Desktop/Hacktoberfest 26/ward`) is a child-owned cyberbullying guardian for the DEV Hacktoberfest Week 4 challenge (deadline 31 Oct 11:59 PM PDT, about 06:59 GMT 1 Nov). Published numbers must match what was actually run, and failures stay published.

Task:
Your area: measurement. Audit items #17 and #18.

Setup: other sessions share this checkout, so work in your own worktree: `git -C ward fetch && git -C ward worktree add "../ward-wt-eval" -b eval-chats origin/main`, `pnpm install`, `node apps/web/scripts/copy-ort.mjs`, and work only there. Check that Ollama is running and which models are pulled.

1. **Fresh Gemma rows.** Rerun the scorecard and the red-team set for Gemma 4 E4B and E2B with the current re-ask code (long runs go in the background). Fix the "one message at a time" label if E4B runs in batches. Add a run date per row and Wilson/bootstrap intervals. If a run can't finish in time, say so instead of guessing.
2. **Chat-level benchmark.** 30 to 40 labelled synthetic chats per language (English, Roman Urdu, Hinglish, Bangla). Include lone threats in a 1:1 DM with and without a reply, sweary friendly banter groups, pile-ons, exclusion, and a child quoting abuse to ask for help. Add `pnpm eval:chats` producing a level confusion matrix (calm / watch / bullying / urgent) plus false-urgent and missed-urgent rates, per tier (word lists only, phone = lists + Ward Lite, computer = + Gemma). Keep the chats out of training: extend the existing leak test. Mark labels as one author's judgement pending native review.
3. **Write it up.** Update `eval/results/`, `docs/REDTEAM.md` (runner-generated parts) and only the scorecard section of `README.md` so the prose matches the tables.

Out of scope: changing engine or classifier behaviour to improve the numbers (another session is changing distress and quoting rules in the engine right now; measure whatever is on main when you run, and note the commit). Run `pnpm test`. Push each piece to main once verified (fetch, rebase onto origin/main, test, push; retry on rejection). Finish with a short report: the headline numbers, commits, and anything surprising, especially missed-urgent cases.

## Does the approach work? The scorecard

Same balanced sample for every system, 200 messages per language, half abusive by each dataset's
own labels. All run locally through Ollama. Method in
[`eval/results/scorecard.md`](eval/results/scorecard.md); rerun with `pnpm eval`.

| Caught (precision) | Word lists only | ShieldGemma 2B | **A phone: word lists + Ward Lite** | Gemma 4 E2B (phone size)\* | **A computer: Gemma 4 E4B**\* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Roman Urdu** | 59% (94%) | 14% (70%) | **83% (86%)**† | 33% (75%) | **86% (86%)** |
| **Bangla** (abuse aimed at a person) | 10% (83%) | 14% (93%) | **46% (79%)** | 34% (71%) | **65% (78%)** |
| **English** (tweet dataset) | 10% (91%) | 19% (73%) | **85% (67%)**† | 33% (69%) | **36% (72%)** |

† **In distribution.** For Roman Urdu and English, Ward Lite was trained on the *train* splits of
the same two datasets the scorecard tests on (it never sees the test messages themselves). The
other systems never saw either dataset. So these two cells show Ward Lite learned those datasets,
not that a phone reads new kinds of chat better than Gemma. **Bangla is the fair comparison:**
Ward Lite's Bangla came from other datasets, and there the computer's Gemma 4 E4B leads, 65% to
46%.

\* **The Gemma rows are from an earlier run** and will be rerun. They were scored before Ward
started asking Gemma again about messages it skipped; in that version Gemma 4 E4B left some
messages without a verdict (81 of 275 on the [red-team set](docs/REDTEAM.md)), and a missing
verdict counts as not caught, so these rows may undercount.

**Ward Lite** is a small classifier we distilled for phones ([`train/`](train/)): 37.7 MB, about 8 ms
per message on one CPU thread of the laptop that ran the scorecard, fully offline. A leak check
dropped 98 training messages that also appear in the scorecard's test sets
([`train/DATA.md`](train/DATA.md)), and in the app it can only *add* warnings, never clear one.

*Written by hand for the first run and rechecked against the tables above on 2026-10-31, after Ward Lite was retrained. The tables are regenerated each run, so check these numbers against them.*

The set is harder than the scorecard on purpose: every message is a trick. On a phone (word lists plus Ward Lite), Ward caught about half the hurtful messages (75 of 142), flagged more than a quarter of the harmless look-alikes (37 of 133), and marked just under half of the dangerous messages as dangerous (18 of 38). The failure classes, worst first:

1. **A child asking for help reads as the bully.** When a child quotes what was said to them ("someone told me to kys and i can't stop thinking about it", "kisi ne mujhe kaha mar jao, mujhe dar lag raha hai", "কেউ আমাকে বলেছে মরে যা, আমার ভয় লাগছে"), the phone flags 10 of 14, and all 5 that quote a self-harm phrase are marked *dangerous* by the word lists. Word lists can't tell quoting from saying; Ward Lite is raise-only, so it can't clear them (it marks two of them dangerous itself); Gemma, which may clear, flagged 12 of 14. In a group chat this is the message where a child tells friends what happened.
2. **Indirect danger in South Asian languages.** "We know where you live" is missed in Roman Urdu, Bangla script and romanised Bangla; "meet me at the gate (or outside) after school, then I'll show you" in Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla script; "everyone would be happier without you" in all four South Asian sets. English has its own: "k y s", "go k!ll urs3lf", "we know which bus you take 🙂". Only 18 of 38 dangerous messages are marked dangerous on a phone (word lists alone: 3).
3. **Sarcasm and backhanded compliments get through.** Word lists 0 of 21, phone 3 of 21, Gemma 9 of 21. "omg congrats on finally getting a friend, so proud of you 🥹", "waah, aaj to tum insaan lag rahi ho 🙂", "বাহ, আজকে তো তোকে মানুষের মতো লাগছে 🙂" pass every phone layer.
4. **Banter and reclaimed words.** The word lists flag all 14 friendly-insult messages (gadha, pagal, idiot, kamina) and 4 of 9 reclaimed ones ("main moti hun aur khush hun"); with Ward Lite added, the phone flags 6 of the 9 reclaimed ones. That is the known limit of the packs layer, and the reason only Gemma may clear a hit; it flagged 7 of the 14 banter messages.
5. **Bangla in Bangla script.** Ward Lite catches 5 of 21 hurtful Bangla-script messages at its 0.48 threshold, against 9 of 19 for the same kinds of message in romanised Bangla. It agrees with the scorecard's weak Bangla and the data card's warning about where the Bangla negatives come from. Gemma skipped 24 of the 41 Bangla-script messages in its run (see Systems).
6. **Game and exam talk marked dangerous.** The retrained Ward Lite no longer marks plans and goodbyes ("can't come today sorry, family dinner 😩", "acha bhai, brb, ammi bula rahi hain", "gate pe milo 4 bajay, samosay khane chalte hain") as dangerous. It still marks 5 of 133 harmless messages dangerous: "watch your back in the game, there's a sniper on the roof", "i'm gonna destroy you in fifa tonight 😤", "kal exam mein phod dunga 💪" and two of the quotes in item 1. With the word lists, 8 of 133 harmless messages are marked dangerous on a phone, and in the app one such message from someone else makes the chat "urgent". Gemma marked 3 harmless messages dangerous, all quotes.
7. **Polite exclusion.** No hostile word, so word lists catch 0 of 23; Ward Lite catches 10 and flags none of the 13 kind look-alikes (Gemma flags 5 of them). This set reads one message at a time: being removed from a group is caught by the pattern engine from WhatsApp events, which isn't tested here.
8. **Spelling disguises.** Word lists catch 18 of 41. Emoji stand-ins (🐷, 🐘, 🐒, 🐄, 🤡: 0 of 7), mixed scripts (an insult in Devanagari or Urdu script inside Roman text, Cyrillic look-alike letters: 0 of 4), an asterisk inside a word ("ch*tiya"), a whole phrase spaced out ("u r a f a t p i g" becomes one long word), three-letter spacing ("k y s": the joining rule needs four letters), and stretched or respelled short words ("marr jaaaaa" and "jaa mar jaa!!" never match "mar ja") all get past the word lists. Ward Lite rescues some on a phone (all 4 mixed-script ones, 2 of the 7 emoji ones), but not "k y s" or "marr jaaaaa".

**Engine issues the first run turned up** (fixed in the engine, not by tuning to this set, unless marked open):

- Fixed: `normalize()` read a "!" (or 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, @, $, |) right after a word as leetspeak, so "idiot!" became "idioti" and a plain insult followed by an exclamation mark was missed. Now only those characters inside or at the start of a word are read as letters. The tables above are from after this fix.
- Fixed in the engine, not yet in the Gemma row above: Gemma 4 E4B, judging 20 messages per request, returned verdicts for only about 70% of them (it leaves out entries, mostly but not only harmless ones), and a missing verdict counted as no opinion. The engine now asks again about skipped messages in groups of 5. The Gemma row here, and the scorecard's Gemma rows, are from before that fix and will be rerun.
- Open: Ward Lite's scores move a little with the other messages in the same batch (danger 0.48 alone, 0.61 next to a longer message, in a spot check), probably from int8 dynamic quantisation. Enough to flip a borderline call.

other systems never saw either dataset. So these two cells show Ward Lite learned those datasets,

per message on one CPU thread of the laptop that ran the scorecard, fully offline. A leak check

content.text:
I pushed three commits to main: 8d7e490 (chat benchmark), b629fb0 (fresh Gemma rows) and 97e7ecb (chat computer tier and README). Everything was measured on the engine as of e547279, which already includes the quoting and distress rules. `pnpm test` passes (70), and the leak tests also pass when pointed at the real training data.

**Message-by-message scorecard** (recall, run 2026-10-31):

| | Phone | Gemma 4 E4B | Gemma 4 E2B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roman Urdu | 83% (in distribution) | 88% | 30% |
| Bangla | 46% (37–56) | 67% (57–75) | 26% |
| English | 85% (in distribution) | 36% | 31% |

- The E4B label now says 20 unrelated messages per request, not one at a time.
- Each row now has its run date and engine commit. Recall and precision carry Wilson intervals, F1 a bootstrap interval.

**Red-team set (142 hurtful messages):** the phone catches 75 and E4B 114 (was 106). E4B left 46 of 275 messages unanswered, down from 81 before the re-ask fix.

**Chat-level benchmark:** 128 chats, 32 per language, labels pending native review. Run with `pnpm eval:chats`.

| | Word lists | Phone | Computer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Right level | 38% | 39% | 72% |
| Missed urgent (of 28) | 23 | 14 | 3 |
| Wrongly called urgent (of 100) | 5 | 21 | 11 |

**Surprises:**
- **E2B loses whole batches, even with the re-ask.** Ollama won't give `gemma4:e2b` structured output, so the engine asks for plain JSON. E2B then writes `"categories": [insult]` without quotes, `parseMessages` in `ollama.ts` rejects the whole reply, and asking again fails the same way. That left 120 of 200 Roman Urdu and 120 of 200 Bangla messages unanswered, so its column undercounts. I didn't fix it because the engine is outside my area; it needs an owner.
- **Computer-tier missed-urgent cases:**
  - bn-31: "মরে যাস না কেন" (why don't you just die) was read as telling them *not* to die.
  - hi-Latn-27 and ur-Latn-27: veiled one-to-one threats ("you'll regret it") were rated hurtful but not dangerous, so those chats showed "watch".
- **Phone:** half the dangerous chats never reach urgent, and only 2 of those 14 still show the message as "not sure".
- **Friend-quoting chats still go urgent on every tier.** The new quoting rule needs the report and the help request in the same message, and in my chats they're split across messages.
- **E4B still flags 13 of 14 red-team help-seekers**, even though its prompt now says quoting for help isn't hostile.
- **The computer tier shows 24 of 40 friendly chats as something other than calm** (17 "watch", 7 "urgent").

In `docs/REDTEAM.md` I updated only the Gemma figures in the hand-written analysis, because the rerun made them false. My notes for the other sessions are in `measurement.md` in the shared notes folder. The `ward-wt-eval` worktree is still there in case a rerun is needed.
